newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-EXECUTION, INTENSITY KEY TO PIVOTAL GAME 5 OF FINALS.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-EXECUTION, INTENSITY KEY TO PIVOTAL GAME 5 OF FINALS.

text.p: There aren't many strategic wrinkles left, so the Utah Jazz and the defending champion Chicago Bulls both expect Wednesday's pivotal Game 5 of the NBA Finals to come down to intensity and execution.

If the Jazz win, they go back to Chicago needing just one more victory to claim the franchise's first championship. But they would still have to win on the road -- something neither team has done yet.
If the Bulls win Wednesday, they would have two chances at home to get their fifth title in seven years.

"We know that they are going to come out and play hard and we expect the same thing of ourselves," Utah's league Most Valuable Player Karl Malone said after practice Tuesday. "How can you not? It's our last game at home and it means a heck of a lot to go back to Chicago up 3-2 rather than down 3-2."
Scottie Pippen was asked if he could imagine Chicago being down 3-2 for the first time ever. "No, not really," he said.
"It feels like that to some degree right now. We lost two games, it's been pretty devastating. Now we have to face them with another game on their home court. They feel pretty confortable right now.
"It's hard to imagine being in that position and hopefully I don't have to see what it feels like," Pippen said.
Game 4's 78-73 result was the lowest Finals points total since the first year of the 24-second clock. With both teams playing great defence, the next score could go even lower.
"That means execution is very important, especially offensively," Michael Jordan said.
"Whoever's going to execute on the offensive end, or control the boards, whoever's going to get into the transition game and get easier baskets, is going to be the winning team."
Asked if this was the strongest challenge the Bulls had faced in their five NBA Finals, Jordan noted that they had also been 2-2 against Portland in 1992 and went on to win 4-2.

But he added: "In terms of talent that we've faced (in the Finals), by far this is the best talent -- from a mature standpoint and the players they have that make up that team. So yeah, in that sense it has to be the biggest challenge that we have faced thus far."
Both teams want to up the emotional ante in Game 5.
"I think it'll be more intensity on both sides of the ball," said Utah's Antoine Carr. "It's going to be wild out there."
Said Chicago coach Phil Jackson: "I think I said yesterday that we have to just have more resolve for 48 minutes.

"We had a great game plan, a great team effort on Sunday. We played the defence we wanted and we had five opportunities at the end of the game in which we didn't score and they got a couple of good defensive plays. That made a difference between ... 3-1 and this being a 2-2 series."
"They're a very hungry basketball team," Pippen said of a Utah team in its first Finals.

"Chasing number five is definitely harder for us. They're challenging us. They're giving us everything we can ask for," added Pippen. "This series is not easy for us. It's more difficult for us than any team we've faced in the Finals.

"I think we're more disappointed than angry," said Pippen. "We realise that we can play better, should play better and we have been in situations where we've played better. We have to have guys step up."
Jackson said he was especially concerned about "the first unit's offensive productivity."
Jordan and Pippen have accounted for nearly 57 percent of Chicago's points in the Finals after combining for just over 48 percent in the regular season.

The Bulls would like other players to carry more of the load -- but there's also always the chance that Jordan, held more or less in check the last two games, might break out with 50 percent or more of his team's offence.

Bryon Russell, who has borne the main brunt of guarding the nine-time scoring champion, was asked if he was afraid of such an explosion. "No, I don't even care," he said. "I'm just going out there to play. He can explode for 60 (points) but as long as we win, then he can have 60."
Jordan got no trips to the foul line Sunday.

"It's obvious that they didn't call any fouls where I could go the free throw line. I was inside a couple of times, evidently they (the Jazz) didn't foul. I think to some degree we have to pound the ball inside," Jordan said.
"That means I have to go inside to some degree and put the pressure on the referees to call the fouls."
